## Arthritis Waiting List Help UK | Rheumatology & Physio
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/arthritis-waiting-list-help
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What can I do while waiting for a rheumatology appointment?
A: Keep gently active, ask about physiotherapy self-referral in your area, track worsening symptoms, and contact your GP surgery if pain, function or sleep get worse so the referral can be reviewed. Waiting times vary by NHS trust.

## Ankylosing Spondylitis (axSpA) | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is ankylosing spondylitis?
A: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), or axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory arthritis mainly affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints. It typically starts in the late teens or twenties with gradual lower back pain and morning stiffness that improves with movement. Daily exercise, physio and biologic drugs keep the spine flexible.
Q: What is the difference between ankylosing spondylitis and axial spondyloarthritis?
A: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is the umbrella term. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the form of axSpA where damage to the sacroiliac joints is visible on an X-ray. Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) is the same condition earlier in its course — visible only on MRI. Treatment is the same for both.
Q: What is the first sign of ankylosing spondylitis?
A: The earliest sign is usually persistent lower back or buttock pain that comes on slowly before age 45, is worse in the morning, lasts over 30 minutes and improves with movement.
Q: Is ankylosing spondylitis a disability?
A: AS is recognised under the UK Equality Act 2010 as it can have a long-term substantial effect on daily activities. Many people qualify for reasonable adjustments at work and may be eligible for PIP.
Q: Can ankylosing spondylitis be cured?
A: There is no cure, but biologics, NSAIDs and daily exercise can keep inflammation under control and prevent spinal damage for most people.
Q: What is the HLA-B27 test?
A: A blood test that checks for the HLA-B27 gene, found in around 90% of UK people with AS. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose AS — it's used alongside symptoms and MRI scans.
Q: Should I exercise if my back hurts?
A: Yes — gentle, regular movement is the single most important treatment for AS. Pain that eases with activity is typical. A physiotherapist can build a safe, progressive programme.

## Elbow Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/elbow-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is elbow arthritis?
A: Elbow arthritis is joint damage in the elbow causing pain, stiffness, locking or grating during movement. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are the main causes. Treatment ranges from activity modification and NSAIDs to arthroscopy or elbow replacement.
Q: What does elbow arthritis feel like?
A: Most people describe a deep ache on the outside or back of the elbow that worsens when straightening the arm fully or carrying a heavy bag. Many lose the last few degrees of extension, so the arm no longer goes completely straight.
Q: Is elbow pain always arthritis?
A: No. The most common causes of elbow pain in UK adults are tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) and golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis) — tendon overload conditions rather than joint arthritis. True elbow arthritis is less common and usually follows an old fracture or develops in people with rheumatoid arthritis.
Q: What is the best exercise for elbow arthritis?
A: Gentle range-of-motion work — bending and straightening the elbow within a pain-free range, plus forearm rotations (palm up, palm down) — is the most evidence-supported routine. Light isometric grip work protects forearm strength without loading the joint.
Q: Should I see a GP about elbow pain?
A: See your GP if elbow pain lasts more than six weeks, wakes you at night, locks or catches, or is accompanied by tingling into the ring and little fingers — that pattern can indicate ulnar nerve irritation that benefits from early treatment.
Q: Can elbow arthritis be cured?
A: Arthritis itself isn't cured, but most people manage symptoms well with exercise, activity modification, topical NSAIDs and occasional corticosteroid injections. Elbow replacement is reserved for severe pain or loss of function and gives good relief in around 85% of cases.

## Fibromyalgia: Symptoms & Management | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/fibromyalgia
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is fibromyalgia?
A: Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition causing widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and 'fibro fog'. It's a disorder of pain processing rather than joint damage. NICE recommends graded exercise, CBT and paced activity as first-line management.
Q: Is fibromyalgia a form of arthritis?
A: No. Fibromyalgia doesn't damage joints or cause inflammation. However, it commonly occurs alongside arthritis and is treated by similar rheumatology teams.
Q: How is fibromyalgia diagnosed in the UK?
A: Diagnosis is clinical — based on widespread pain lasting over 3 months, plus fatigue, sleep and cognitive symptoms. Blood tests are used to rule out other conditions.
Q: What is fibro fog?
A: Fibro fog is the cognitive symptom of fibromyalgia — short-term memory lapses, word-finding difficulties and trouble concentrating. It improves with better sleep, pacing and exercise.
Q: Can fibromyalgia be cured?
A: There is no cure, but with self-management, exercise, medication and CBT, many people significantly reduce symptoms and stay in work and family life.
Q: Does fibromyalgia get worse over time?
A: Fibromyalgia is not progressive — it doesn't damage tissue. Symptoms fluctuate, often worsening with stress, poor sleep or overdoing activity, and easing with steady self-management.

## Gout: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/gout
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is gout?
A: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by high uric acid crystallising inside joints — usually the big toe — triggering sudden severe pain, redness and swelling. UK guidelines recommend urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) after a second attack to prevent joint damage. Diet and alcohol adjustments help.
Q: What are the first signs of gout?
A: The first sign is usually a sudden, severe attack of pain in a single joint — most often the big toe — that wakes you up at night. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and so tender that even the weight of a bedsheet feels unbearable. Attacks typically peak within 24 hours.
Q: How do I know if my toe pain is gout?
A: Gout in the big toe (called podagra) comes on suddenly, usually overnight, with intense burning pain, redness, heat and swelling at the base of the toe. If you can't bear weight on it or even touch it, and the attack settles over 3–10 days, gout is the most likely cause. A blood test for uric acid and joint fluid analysis can confirm it.
Q: What does a gout attack feel like?
A: Most people describe a sudden, intense burning or throbbing pain in one joint — often the big toe — that starts overnight. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and so tender that even a bedsheet can be unbearable.
Q: Is gout curable?
A: Gout itself is a long-term condition, but with allopurinol or febuxostat plus diet and lifestyle changes, most people stop having attacks completely.
Q: What foods should I avoid with gout?
A: Limit red meat, organ meats, shellfish, oily fish (anchovies, sardines), beer, spirits and sugary drinks. Cherries, water and low-fat dairy can help reduce attacks.
Q: How long does a gout attack last?
A: An untreated attack peaks at 24 hours and usually settles within 3 to 10 days. NSAIDs or colchicine started early can shorten and ease attacks.
Q: Is gout the same as arthritis?
A: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by uric-acid crystals, distinct from osteoarthritis (wear and tear) or rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune).

## Hand Arthritis: Symptoms & Exercises | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/hand-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is hand arthritis?
A: Hand arthritis affects the small joints of the fingers, thumbs and wrists. Osteoarthritis typically causes bony bumps and thumb-base pain; rheumatoid usually causes symmetrical knuckle swelling. Splints, hand exercises and topical NSAID gels help most people.
Q: What are the first signs of hand arthritis?
A: Early signs include stiffness in the fingers in the morning, a dull ache at the base of the thumb when opening jars or turning keys, and small bony lumps on the end finger joints (Heberden's nodes).
Q: What is the best exercise for arthritic hands?
A: A daily 5-minute routine of fist-to-fan, finger-to-thumb touches, and gentle putty squeezes maintains range of motion and grip strength without overloading inflamed joints.
Q: Do hand splints actually help?
A: Yes — for thumb base (CMC) arthritis, a custom or off-the-shelf neoprene splint reduces pain during pinching tasks and is recommended by NICE as part of first-line care.
Q: Are the bony lumps on my fingers permanent?
A: Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes are bone changes and don't shrink, but the pain associated with their formation usually settles within 1–2 years. The remaining stiffness can be managed with exercise.
Q: When is hand surgery needed?
A: Surgery (most commonly trapeziectomy for thumb base arthritis or joint fusion for severe finger OA) is reserved for persistent pain that hasn't responded to splinting, exercise, injections and topical NSAIDs over 6+ months.

## Hip Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/hip-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is hip arthritis?
A: Hip arthritis is joint damage — usually osteoarthritis — of the hip, causing groin or buttock pain, stiffness and difficulty putting on socks or shoes. Physio-led strengthening, weight management and, when severe, hip replacement (over 100,000 done in the UK each year) provide long-term relief.
Q: What does hip arthritis feel like?
A: Most people feel a deep ache in the groin or front of the hip that worsens with walking, standing up from a chair, or putting on socks. Stiffness is common after sitting and first thing in the morning, usually easing within 30 minutes of moving.
Q: How do I relieve hip pain while sleeping?
A: Sleep on your back or on the unaffected side with a firm pillow between your knees to keep the hips aligned. A medium-firm mattress, a warm bath before bed, and a topical NSAID gel applied to the hip help reduce night pain. Avoid sleeping on the painful side and don't tuck your top knee in front of the bottom one — it twists the joint.
Q: What is the best exercise for hip arthritis?
A: Glute and hip-abductor strengthening (bridges, clams, side-lying leg raises) combined with low-impact cardio such as cycling, swimming or pool walking is the most evidence-based approach. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for everyone with hip OA.
Q: Should I keep walking with hip arthritis?
A: Yes. Regular walking strengthens the muscles that support the hip and reduces pain over time. Build up gradually, wear cushioned shoes, and use a walking pole in the hand opposite to the painful hip to offload the joint by up to 25%.
Q: When is a hip replacement needed?
A: Hip replacement is usually considered when pain disturbs sleep, severely limits walking or daily activity, and conservative measures (exercise, weight management, painkillers, injections) have not worked over several months. UK outcomes are excellent — over 95% of hip replacements still function well at 10 years.
Q: Does losing weight help hip arthritis?
A: Yes. The hip carries roughly three times body weight when walking and up to five times when climbing stairs, so even small weight loss meaningfully reduces joint load and pain.

## Juvenile Arthritis (JIA) in Children | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/juvenile-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is juvenile arthritis?
A: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is arthritis starting before age 16, lasting more than 6 weeks. It affects around 1 in 1,000 UK children. Early paediatric rheumatology care and DMARDs help most children live active lives.
Q: What are the first signs of arthritis in a child?
A: Look out for limping (worse in the morning), a swollen joint, a child avoiding a normally favourite activity, or unexplained fevers and rashes. Always see your GP if joint symptoms last more than two weeks.
Q: Is juvenile arthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis?
A: No. JIA is its own group of conditions. Some forms behave similarly to rheumatoid arthritis, but JIA also includes types not seen in adults, such as systemic JIA (Still's disease).
Q: Will my child grow out of JIA?
A: Some children — particularly those with oligoarticular JIA — do go into long-term remission. Others have ongoing disease into adulthood. Modern treatments have transformed the outlook for most.
Q: Why does my child need eye checks?
A: JIA can cause silent eye inflammation (uveitis) that, if missed, can damage sight. Regular slit-lamp checks by an ophthalmologist are essential.
Q: Can my child still play sport?
A: Yes — sport is encouraged. Swimming and cycling are particularly good. Adapt during flares and work with the rheumatology team and PE staff.

## Knee Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/knee-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is knee arthritis?
A: Knee arthritis is joint damage in the knee — most often osteoarthritis — causing pain when standing, walking or climbing stairs, stiffness after rest, and swelling. NICE recommends exercise and weight loss as first-line treatment; every 5 kg lost cuts knee load by roughly 20 kg.
Q: What's the best exercise for knee arthritis?
A: Quadriceps strengthening (straight-leg raises, wall sits) plus low-impact aerobic (cycling, swimming). 3-5 sessions a week for 8+ weeks shows meaningful pain reduction.
Q: Should I use a walking stick?
A: Use it in the opposite hand to the painful knee — this reduces load by up to 25%.

## Lupus (SLE): Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/lupus
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is lupus?
A: Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, heart and lungs. Common symptoms include joint pain, a butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity. Hydroxychloroquine is the mainstay of treatment.
Q: Is lupus a form of arthritis?
A: Lupus isn't classed as arthritis but it commonly causes joint pain and stiffness. Many people are managed by the same rheumatology teams that treat rheumatoid arthritis.
Q: Can lupus be cured?
A: There is no cure, but modern treatments — particularly hydroxychloroquine — control symptoms and reduce flares for most people. Many achieve long periods of remission.
Q: What is the butterfly rash?
A: A flat or slightly raised red rash across the cheeks and bridge of the nose, in the shape of a butterfly. It is one of the most recognisable signs of lupus, though not everyone develops it.
Q: Why is sun protection so important with lupus?
A: UV light can trigger lupus flares — both skin rashes and internal symptoms. Daily SPF 50, UV-protective clothing and hats are essential, even on cloudy UK days.
Q: Can people with lupus have children?
A: Yes. Pregnancy in lupus needs to be planned with your rheumatology and obstetric team, ideally during a period of stable disease, with medications reviewed in advance.

## Osteoarthritis: Symptoms, Treatment & Exercises | UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is osteoarthritis?
A: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis in the UK. It happens when protective cartilage on the ends of your bones wears down over time, most often in knees, hips, hands and spine. Symptoms include joint pain that worsens with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, swelling and reduced movement. It's manageable with exercise, weight control, and, when needed, medication or joint replacement.
Q: Can osteoarthritis be reversed?
A: No, cartilage loss can't currently be reversed, but symptoms and progression can be significantly slowed with exercise, weight management and joint-friendly activity.
Q: What's the best exercise for osteoarthritis?
A: Low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming) plus strength training around the affected joint. NICE recommends 30 minutes most days.
Q: Does osteoarthritis show on an X-ray?
A: Yes — X-rays show joint space narrowing and bone spurs, though symptoms don't always match imaging severity.
Q: When should I see a GP?
A: If joint pain limits daily activity, wakes you at night, or hasn't improved after 6 weeks of self-management, book a GP appointment.

## Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is polymyalgia rheumatica?
A: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) causes sudden shoulder and hip stiffness and pain, mainly in adults over 50. Low-dose steroids (prednisolone 15 mg) usually give dramatic relief within days. Treatment typically continues for 1-2 years.
Q: How is polymyalgia rheumatica diagnosed in the UK?
A: Your GP will check your symptoms, examine your shoulders and hips, and arrange blood tests (CRP and ESR) to look for inflammation. A dramatic improvement within a few days of starting prednisolone helps confirm the diagnosis.
Q: How long does polymyalgia rheumatica last?
A: Most people need steroid treatment for 1 to 3 years. Around half of those affected have one or more flares during the taper, but the condition usually goes into long-term remission.
Q: Is polymyalgia rheumatica an autoimmune disease?
A: Yes — PMR is driven by an overactive immune response that inflames the lining of joints and bursae, particularly in the shoulders and hips. It is not contagious and is not caused by anything you have done.
Q: What is the link with giant cell arteritis?
A: Around 1 in 5 people with PMR also develop giant cell arteritis (GCA), which inflames blood vessels in the head. New headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, or any change in vision need urgent medical attention.
Q: Can I exercise with polymyalgia rheumatica?
A: Yes, and you should. Gentle walking, shoulder and hip mobility work, and light resistance training protect muscle and bone during long-term steroid use. Start slowly and build up.
Q: Are there natural alternatives to steroids for PMR?
A: There is no proven natural alternative to steroids for PMR — untreated inflammation can damage tissue and increase the risk of GCA. A Mediterranean diet, exercise and bone-protection medicines support steroid treatment rather than replace it.

## Psoriatic Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is psoriatic arthritis?
A: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis that affects around 1 in 5 people with psoriasis. It causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness — often in fingers, toes, lower back or knees — plus nail changes and skin plaques. Early diagnosis and DMARDs or biologics prevent joint damage.
Q: Can you have PsA without psoriasis?
A: Yes, about 15% of people develop joint symptoms before skin symptoms. Family history and nail pitting are clues.
Q: Is psoriatic arthritis worse than rheumatoid arthritis?
A: Both can cause serious joint damage. PsA has more variable patterns; RA is usually more symmetrical. Outcomes depend on early treatment.

## Reactive Arthritis: Causes & Recovery | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/reactive-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is reactive arthritis?
A: Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body — usually gut or urinary. Symptoms include joint pain, eye inflammation and urinary symptoms. Most cases resolve within 3-12 months.
Q: How long does reactive arthritis last?
A: Most people recover fully within 3 to 6 months. Around 1 in 5 develop longer-lasting joint problems, and a smaller number go on to develop a chronic inflammatory arthritis, which is why early specialist input matters.
Q: Is reactive arthritis curable?
A: Yes — for most people reactive arthritis settles completely once the triggering infection clears and inflammation is treated. NSAIDs, joint injections and physiotherapy speed recovery.
Q: Can reactive arthritis come back?
A: It can. People with the HLA-B27 gene are more likely to have repeat episodes, often triggered by a new gut or urinary infection. Practising food hygiene and safer sex reduces the risk.
Q: How is reactive arthritis diagnosed in the UK?
A: Your GP will ask about recent gut, urinary or chest infections and examine your joints, eyes and skin. Blood tests (CRP, ESR, HLA-B27), urine tests and sometimes joint fluid analysis or imaging are used to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other arthritis.
Q: Is reactive arthritis contagious?
A: No. Reactive arthritis itself cannot be passed from person to person. However, the infections that trigger it (such as chlamydia or salmonella) can be — so treating partners and practising good food hygiene matters.
Q: What is the difference between reactive arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
A: Reactive arthritis is triggered by a recent infection, usually affects one or a few large joints, and most people recover within months. Rheumatoid arthritis is a lifelong autoimmune disease that typically affects small joints on both sides of the body and needs long-term medication.

## Rheumatoid Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
A: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of your joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness — usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet). Early treatment with DMARDs (disease-modifying drugs) within 3 months of symptoms starting can prevent joint damage. It affects about 400,000 adults in the UK.
Q: Is rheumatoid arthritis a disability?
A: It can qualify as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it substantially affects daily activities. Many people with RA are eligible for PIP.
Q: What's the difference between OA and RA?
A: OA is wear-and-tear cartilage loss. RA is an autoimmune inflammatory disease. RA usually affects joints symmetrically and causes prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour).
Q: Can diet help RA?
A: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in oily fish, olive oil and vegetables can reduce inflammatory markers. It doesn't replace DMARDs but supports overall control.

## Shoulder Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/conditions/shoulder-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is shoulder arthritis?
A: Shoulder arthritis is cartilage loss in the glenohumeral or acromioclavicular joints, causing deep aching pain, reduced reach and night pain when lying on the affected side. Physio, corticosteroid injections and, if severe, shoulder replacement are options.
Q: What does shoulder arthritis feel like?
A: Most people describe a deep ache at the back of the shoulder that worsens when reaching overhead, behind the back, or lying on that side at night. Stiffness limits putting on coats and reaching seatbelts.
Q: Is shoulder arthritis the same as a frozen shoulder?
A: No. Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is inflammation of the joint capsule and usually resolves within 1–3 years. Shoulder arthritis is cartilage wear and is progressive — but both can cause similar early symptoms, so accurate diagnosis matters.
Q: What is the best exercise for shoulder arthritis?
A: Pendulum swings, doorway stretches and gentle external rotation with a resistance band are the most evidence-supported exercises. They protect range of motion and rotator cuff strength without overloading the joint.
Q: Should I get an injection in my shoulder?
A: Corticosteroid injections can give 6–12 weeks of meaningful pain relief and are useful to bridge a flare or to allow physiotherapy to progress. Most clinicians limit injections to 2–3 per year.
Q: When is shoulder replacement needed?
A: Shoulder replacement is considered when night pain is severe, function is limited despite physiotherapy and injections, and X-rays confirm advanced joint changes. The reverse total shoulder replacement is the most common option in the UK.

## Best Arthritis Diet UK | Anti-Inflammatory Foods
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/diet
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is the best diet for arthritis?
A: A Mediterranean-style pattern has the strongest evidence: plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, olive oil, nuts and oily fish twice a week, with less red and processed meat, added sugar and ultra-processed food. For weight-bearing joints, losing excess weight lowers the load through the joint. No food cures arthritis.

## Diet & Nutrition Hub for Arthritis | UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/diet-hub
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What's the best diet for arthritis?
A: A Mediterranean diet — oily fish twice a week, olive oil, nuts, wholegrains, plenty of vegetables and fruit — consistently reduces inflammation markers and joint pain in trials. Cut ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks and excess red meat. Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain.

## Exercise Hub: Arthritis-Friendly Workouts | UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/exercise-hub
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What's the best exercise for arthritis?
A: Combine aerobic (walking, swimming, cycling) with strength training 2-3 times a week and flexibility work. NICE guideline NG226 recommends exercise as first-line for all arthritis types — with pain reduction comparable to NSAIDs and no side effects.

## Arthritis Glossary: 110+ UK Terms Explained
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What arthritis and rheumatology terms should I know?
A: Living With Arthritis UK's plain-English glossary covers 110+ terms across rheumatology, musculoskeletal medicine, treatment, imaging, benefits and self-management — from DMARDs and biologics through DAS28, HLA-B27, sarcopenia and frailty. Every term is medically reviewed and linked to related conditions and guides so you can quickly understand your diagnosis, appointment letters or research articles.

## ACR20/50/70: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/acr-response
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is acr20/50/70?
A: ACR20/50/70: ACR response criteria (American College of Rheumatology) measure whether patients improve 20%, 50% or 70% in RA trials. Used to compare drugs but rarely quoted directly in NHS clinics.

## ACT: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/act-therapy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is act?
A: ACT: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a psychological approach for chronic pain that focuses on living well with pain rather than eliminating it. Growing NICE endorsement for chronic primary pain. Available via NHS Talking Therapies.

## Acupuncture: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/acupuncture
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is acupuncture?
A: Acupuncture: Acupuncture uses thin needles at specific body points. NICE no longer recommends it for OA (evidence downgraded), but some people find it helpful for chronic pain as part of a broader plan. Rarely available on NHS for arthritis.

## Adalimumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/adalimumab
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is adalimumab?
A: Adalimumab: Adalimumab is a biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, used for RA, PsA, AS and other inflammatory conditions. Self-injected every 1-2 weeks. Biosimilars are widely used in the NHS. Screening for TB, hepatitis and current infections is essential before starting.

## Allopurinol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/allopurinol
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is allopurinol?
A: Allopurinol: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production and prevents future gout attacks. Started at low dose after the acute attack settles, titrated up over months. Target: uric acid <360 μmol/L, or <300 with tophi.

## Amitriptyline: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/amitriptyline
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is amitriptyline?
A: Amitriptyline: Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25 mg at night) is a common NHS prescription for chronic pain including fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain. Improves sleep and reduces pain sensitivity. Not addictive but takes weeks to work.

## Ankylosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/ankylosis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is ankylosis?
A: Ankylosis: Ankylosis is stiffening or fusion of a joint, either bony (in ankylosing spondylitis) or fibrous. Untreated inflammation and immobility promote it. Prevention through medication and exercise is far more effective than reversal.

## Anti-CCP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/anti-ccp
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is anti-ccp?
A: Anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor for diagnosing RA. Positive anti-CCP predicts more aggressive disease and helps rheumatologists decide on early aggressive treatment.

## Arthrodesis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/arthrodesis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is arthrodesis?
A: Arthrodesis: Arthrodesis fuses bones in a joint together, eliminating movement to eliminate pain. Sometimes done in ankles, wrists, spine and small joints when replacement isn't suitable. Trades movement for pain relief.

## Arthroscopy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/arthroscopy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is arthroscopy?
A: Arthroscopy: Arthroscopy is keyhole surgery to diagnose or treat problems inside a joint. Small incisions, thin camera. NICE no longer recommends 'clean-out' arthroscopy for OA — evidence showed no benefit — but it remains useful for specific mechanical problems.

## Attendance Allowance | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/attendance-allowance
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is attendance allowance?
A: Attendance Allowance: Attendance Allowance is a non-means-tested benefit for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of illness or disability. £68.10-£101.75/week (2025 rates). Doesn't require an assessment of ability to walk.

## Biologic: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/biologic
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is biologic?
A: Biologic: Biologics are targeted immune-system drugs used when conventional DMARDs alone don't control inflammatory arthritis. UK NICE approves them based on disease activity scores. Examples: adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab, rituximab. They increase infection risk so vaccinations and screening are essential.

## Bisphosphonates: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/bisphosphonates
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is bisphosphonates?
A: Bisphosphonates: Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate, zoledronic acid) slow bone breakdown and reduce fracture risk in osteoporosis. Weekly tablet or annual infusion. Take on an empty stomach, stay upright 30 min. Rare jaw and thigh bone side effects.

## Blue Badge: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/blue-badge
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is blue badge?
A: Blue Badge: The Blue Badge is a UK-wide parking scheme giving concessions to people with severe walking difficulty. Automatic eligibility with higher-rate PIP mobility; discretionary applications also possible. Fee £10 in England, free in Wales/Scotland.

## BMI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/bmi
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is bmi?
A: BMI: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. Rough guide only — doesn't distinguish muscle from fat. NHS categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 healthy, 25-29.9 overweight, 30+ obese.

## Bone density (BMD) | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/bone-density
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is bone density (bmd)?
A: Bone density (BMD): Bone mineral density is measured by DEXA scan, expressed as a T-score. Below -1: osteopenia; below -2.5: osteoporosis. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D and, when needed, bisphosphonates maintain BMD.

## Bone scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/bone-scan
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is bone scan?
A: Bone scan: A bone (bone scintigraphy) scan uses a small dose of radioactive tracer taken up by active bone. Used for detecting metastases, hidden fractures, complex regional pain syndrome and bone infections.

## Capsaicin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/capsaicin
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is capsaicin?
A: Capsaicin: Capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) desensitises pain nerves over 2-4 weeks of regular application. NICE-recommended for OA hand and knee. Available on NHS prescription. Wash hands after use.

## Cartilage: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/cartilage
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is cartilage?
A: Cartilage: Cartilage is the smooth, tough connective tissue capping the ends of bones where they meet in joints. It cushions impact and allows friction-free movement. In osteoarthritis, cartilage gradually thins and roughens; it has no direct blood supply so heals slowly.

## CBD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/cbd
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is cbd?
A: CBD: CBD is a non-psychoactive cannabis compound sold in the UK as an over-the-counter supplement. Evidence for arthritis pain relief is preliminary. Legally sold if <0.2% THC. Not the same as prescribed medical cannabis.

## Clinical Frailty Scale | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/cfs
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is clinical frailty scale?
A: Clinical Frailty Scale: The Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale rates frailty 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Used across the NHS in hospital admissions and community care. Scores 1-3 fit; 4-5 vulnerable; 6+ frail.

## Codeine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/codeine
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is codeine?
A: Codeine: Codeine is a weak opioid, often combined with paracetamol (co-codamol). Constipation is universal; addiction risk with regular use. NICE increasingly cautions against long-term opioid use in chronic non-cancer pain.

## Colchicine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/colchicine
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is colchicine?
A: Colchicine: Colchicine is used for acute gout when NSAIDs aren't suitable. Effective if started early in the attack. Dose reduced from historical high doses because of side effects.

## Corticosteroid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/corticosteroid
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is corticosteroid?
A: Corticosteroid: Corticosteroids (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone) rapidly reduce inflammation but have long-term side effects: weight gain, high blood sugar, bone thinning, mood changes. Used short-term for flares or as targeted joint injections.

## Crepitus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/crepitus
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is crepitus?
A: Crepitus: Crepitus is the audible or palpable grating, crackling or clicking felt when a joint moves. Common in OA and often harmless in isolation — many people over 40 have crepitus without pain. Concerning if painful or new.

## CRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/crp
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is crp?
A: CRP: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation. Rises faster than ESR (hours vs days) and drops more quickly when inflammation resolves. Used to monitor flares and treatment response in inflammatory arthritis.

## CT scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/ct-scan
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is ct scan?
A: CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to build detailed cross-sectional bone images. Better than plain X-ray for complex fractures and bony detail; poorer than MRI for soft tissue. Uses ionising radiation.

## Dactylitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/dactylitis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is dactylitis?
A: Dactylitis: Dactylitis is swelling of a whole digit ('sausage finger' or 'sausage toe') from combined joint and tendon inflammation. Highly characteristic of psoriatic and reactive arthritis. Requires rheumatology assessment.

## DAS28: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/das28
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is das28?
A: DAS28: The Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) is used by UK rheumatology to decide treatment escalation. Combines tender joints, swollen joints, ESR/CRP and patient global rating. NICE thresholds determine biologic eligibility.

## DAS28 remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/das28-remission
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is das28 remission?
A: DAS28 remission: DAS28 < 2.6 is the standard definition of RA remission. Achievable in around half of people on early aggressive treatment. Goal of modern RA management.

## DASS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/dass-score
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is dass?
A: DASS: DASS is a self-report questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and stress. Used to identify mental health impact of chronic conditions like arthritis. NHS Talking Therapies uses similar tools to guide treatment.

## DEXA scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/dexa-scan
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is dexa scan?
A: DEXA scan: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density at hip and spine. Standard test for osteoporosis diagnosis. Low radiation dose. NHS available on GP or specialist referral.

## DMARD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/dmard
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is dmard?
A: DMARD: DMARDs are drugs that slow the underlying disease process in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, JIA). Conventional DMARDs include methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide. Starting a DMARD within 3 months of RA symptoms significantly reduces long-term joint damage. All require regular blood monitoring.

## Enthesitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/enthesitis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is enthesitis?
A: Enthesitis: Enthesitis is inflammation at the entheses — where tendons or ligaments attach to bone. Characteristic of spondyloarthropathies (AS, PsA) and often the first symptom (e.g. Achilles tendon pain, plantar fasciitis).

## Epidural: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/epidural
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is epidural?
A: Epidural: Epidural steroid injections deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to the spine for radiculopathy (nerve root pain). NICE recommends caution — some benefit for acute severe sciatica, limited role in chronic back pain.

## Erythema migrans: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/erythema-migrans
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is erythema migrans?
A: Erythema migrans: Erythema migrans is the classic expanding 'bulls-eye' rash of early Lyme disease. Antibiotics started early prevent Lyme arthritis and other complications. If you develop joint pain after a tick bite and rash, see your GP promptly.

## ESR: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/esr
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is esr?
A: ESR: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube, indirectly indicating inflammation. Elevated in inflammatory arthritis, infections, and other conditions. Used alongside CRP to monitor disease activity, not for diagnosis alone.

## Etanercept: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/etanercept
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is etanercept?
A: Etanercept: Etanercept is a TNF-blocking biologic self-injected weekly or twice weekly. Widely used in the UK for RA, PsA, AS and juvenile arthritis. NHS eligibility depends on disease activity scores (DAS28).

## Facet joint injection | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/facet-joint-injection
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is facet joint injection?
A: Facet joint injection: Facet joint injections deliver local anaesthetic and steroid to the small joints at the back of the spine. Used for suspected facet-mediated back pain. Evidence for lasting benefit is mixed.

## Falls risk: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/falls-risk
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is falls risk?
A: Falls risk: Falls risk in older adults with arthritis is doubled by pain, weakness, poor balance, medications and vision. Assessed via history (previous falls, near-falls), timed-up-and-go test, and medication review. Halveable with structured intervention.

## Flare: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/flare
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is flare?
A: Flare: A flare is a sudden or gradual worsening of arthritis symptoms — more pain, stiffness, swelling and fatigue — lasting days to weeks. Common triggers: stress, illness, over-exertion, weather changes, missed medication. Have a written flare plan agreed with your rheumatology team.

## Frailty: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/frailty
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is frailty?
A: Frailty: Frailty is not the same as ageing — it's reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to setbacks. Assessed with tools like the Clinical Frailty Scale. Reversible early: strength training, protein, treating cataracts, medication review.

## FRAX score: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/frax
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is frax score?
A: FRAX score: FRAX is an online tool from Sheffield University that estimates your 10-year risk of hip and major fracture based on age, sex, BMI, family and clinical factors. Used by NHS GPs to decide who needs bone-density scanning or treatment.

## Gabapentin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/gabapentin
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is gabapentin?
A: Gabapentin: Gabapentin has similar uses to pregabalin (nerve pain, fibromyalgia). Also a controlled drug in the UK. Cheaper than pregabalin. Titrated up over weeks; withdrawal must be gradual.

## Gout attack: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/gout-attack
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is gout attack?
A: Gout attack: A gout attack is sudden severe joint pain, swelling and redness, most often in the big toe. Peaks within 24 hours. Treated with NSAIDs, colchicine or short steroid course. Recurrent attacks need urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol).

## GP referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/gp-referral
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is gp referral?
A: GP referral: GP referral is the standard NHS route to see a specialist (rheumatologist, orthopaedic surgeon). For MSK physio, many areas now allow self-referral without GP. Waiting times for rheumatology first appointment: 4-30 weeks depending on area.

## Hip replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/hip-replacement
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is hip replacement?
A: Hip replacement: Hip replacement (arthroplasty) replaces the worn-out hip with metal, ceramic and plastic components. Around 100,000 done in the UK yearly. Excellent outcomes for pain and function; modern implants last 20+ years for most.

## HLA-B27: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/hla-b27
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is hla-b27?
A: HLA-B27: HLA-B27 is a genetic marker present in ~90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis, but also in ~8% of the general UK population without disease. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose disease — clinical assessment and imaging are essential.

## Hydrotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/hydrotherapy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is hydrotherapy?
A: Hydrotherapy: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool (33-36°C). Water reduces joint load and warmth eases pain, allowing movement that isn't possible on land. NHS access varies; some rheumatology units offer courses.

## Hydroxychloroquine | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/hydroxychloroquine
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is hydroxychloroquine?
A: Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a well-tolerated DMARD used in lupus, mild RA and combination therapy. Requires annual eye checks because of a small long-term retinal risk. Safe in pregnancy.

## NHS Talking Therapies | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/iapt
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is nhs talking therapies?
A: NHS Talking Therapies: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) provides free CBT, counselling and mindfulness-based therapy for adults with anxiety, depression and chronic pain. Self-referral online in most areas. Waiting times variable.

## Infliximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/infliximab
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is infliximab?
A: Infliximab: Infliximab is a biologic given by hospital infusion every 6-8 weeks. Used in RA, PsA, AS, Crohn's and other conditions. Requires ongoing hospital appointments but effective and predictable.

## JAK inhibitor: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/jak-inhibitor
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is jak inhibitor?
A: JAK inhibitor: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are oral drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune signalling pathway. Highly effective in RA and PsA. UK regulators have restricted use in some groups because of cardiovascular and cancer safety data.

## Joint effusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/joint-effusion
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is joint effusion?
A: Joint effusion: A joint effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule, causing visible swelling, tightness and reduced movement. Common in OA, RA, gout, trauma or infection. May be drained (aspirated) to relieve symptoms and analyse the cause.

## Kinesiology tape: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/kinesiology-tape
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is kinesiology tape?
A: Kinesiology tape: Kinesiology tape is elastic tape applied by physiotherapists to support joints without restricting movement. Evidence for specific pain relief is limited, but many people report benefit as part of a broader rehab plan.

## Knee replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/knee-replacement
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is knee replacement?
A: Knee replacement: Knee replacement replaces the worn joint surfaces. Total knee replacement is more common than partial. Recovery: hospital stay 1-3 days, walking with aid within weeks, full recovery 6-12 months. Physio before and after is critical.

## Labrum: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/labrum
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is labrum?
A: Labrum: The labrum is the ring of cartilage around the hip and shoulder sockets, deepening the joint and helping stability. Tears can cause pain and clicking. Some are surgically treated but many respond to physiotherapy.

## Leflunomide: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/leflunomide
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is leflunomide?
A: Leflunomide: Leflunomide is an oral DMARD for RA and PsA when methotrexate isn't tolerated or effective. Requires regular blood monitoring and effective contraception in men and women (long half-life).

## Medical cannabis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/medical-cannabis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is medical cannabis?
A: Medical cannabis: Medical cannabis has been legal on prescription in the UK since 2018 but is very rarely prescribed for arthritis — usually reserved for specific licensed conditions (severe epilepsy, chemotherapy nausea, MS spasticity).

## Meniscus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/meniscus
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is meniscus?
A: Meniscus: The meniscus is a C-shaped cartilage disc in the knee that cushions and stabilises the joint. Age-related tears are common and often symptomless. NICE recommends physiotherapy first for degenerative tears — surgery only for specific mechanical symptoms.

## Methotrexate: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/methotrexate
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is methotrexate?
A: Methotrexate: Methotrexate is the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis and many inflammatory conditions, usually taken once weekly with folic acid on other days. Requires regular blood tests. Common side effects (nausea, tiredness) often improve after a few months.

## Morning stiffness | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/morning-stiffness
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is morning stiffness?
A: Morning stiffness: Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes is typical of osteoarthritis. Stiffness over an hour, especially symmetrical, points to inflammatory arthritis like RA and needs urgent GP review. Duration is a key diagnostic clue.

## Morphine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/morphine
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is morphine?
A: Morphine: Strong opioids like morphine are rarely used in chronic arthritis because evidence for long-term benefit is poor and risks (dependence, falls, respiratory depression) are high. Occasionally used short-term for severe flares or post-op.

## MRI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/mri
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is mri?
A: MRI: MRI uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue and bone marrow in detail. Best for cartilage, ligaments, tendons and early inflammatory changes not visible on X-ray. No radiation. NHS waiting times vary.

## Musculoskeletal (MSK) | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/musculoskeletal
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is musculoskeletal (msk)?
A: Musculoskeletal (MSK): 'Musculoskeletal' means anything involving muscles, bones, joints, tendons or ligaments. MSK conditions are the leading cause of work absence and disability in the UK, affecting around 20 million people. Most GP visits for back pain, joint pain and sports injuries are MSK.

## NICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/nice
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is nice?
A: NICE: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) develops evidence-based guidelines for the NHS in England (and adopted by Wales/NI). Key arthritis guidelines: NG226 (OA), NG100 (RA), CG79 (RA in adults). Your care should broadly follow NICE guidance.

## NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/nsaid
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is nsaid?
A: NSAID: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but carry stomach, kidney and heart risk with sustained use. NICE recommends topical NSAIDs first for hand/knee OA. Take with food; check with pharmacist if over 65, taking blood thinners, or with kidney/heart conditions.

## Topical NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/nsaid-topical
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is topical nsaid?
A: Topical NSAID: Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen gel, diclofenac gel) are applied to the skin over a painful joint. NICE first-line for hand and knee OA — comparable pain relief to oral NSAIDs but far lower systemic risk.

## Occupational therapy | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/occupational-therapy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is occupational therapy?
A: Occupational therapy: Occupational therapists (OTs) help with practical daily activities — dressing, cooking, work, hobbies — using adapted techniques, aids and equipment. NHS OTs assess your home and provide equipment such as grab rails free of charge.

## Orthotics: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/orthotics
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is orthotics?
A: Orthotics: Orthotics are custom or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that change how weight passes through the foot, ankle, knee and hip. Helpful for hallux valgus, flat feet, plantar fasciitis and some knee OA. NHS podiatry can prescribe them.

## Osteophyte: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/osteophyte
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is osteophyte?
A: Osteophyte: Osteophytes ('bone spurs') are bony outgrowths at the edges of joints damaged by osteoarthritis. Show clearly on X-rays. They can restrict movement and, in the spine, sometimes press on nerves — but many are painless.

## Osteoporosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/osteoporosis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is osteoporosis?
A: Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is silently reduced bone density until a fragility fracture happens. Screening after menopause or long-term steroid use. Managed with lifestyle, calcium, vitamin D and bisphosphonates (alendronic acid) if high risk.

## Osteotomy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/osteotomy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is osteotomy?
A: Osteotomy: Osteotomy cuts and realigns bone to shift load onto a healthier part of the joint. Sometimes used in younger patients with unilateral knee OA to delay replacement. Now less common with modern replacement techniques.

## Otago exercise programme | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/otago
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is otago exercise programme?
A: Otago exercise programme: The Otago Exercise Programme is a physiotherapy-designed home programme of leg strength and balance exercises. Randomised trial evidence shows ~35% fewer falls in older adults. Available through NHS falls services.

## Pain scale (0-10) | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/pain-scale
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is pain scale (0-10)?
A: Pain scale (0-10): The 0-10 numeric pain rating is used in NHS clinics to track pain over time. 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable. Useful for consultation, less useful for diagnosis (subjective).

## Pannus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/pannus
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is pannus?
A: Pannus: Pannus is abnormal granulation tissue that grows in RA-affected joints, releasing enzymes that erode cartilage and bone. Early effective DMARD treatment prevents pannus formation and the resulting joint damage.

## Passive vs active movement | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is passive vs active movement?
A: Passive vs active movement: Passive movement is when a therapist moves your joint through its range without you contracting muscles. Active movement is when you do it yourself. Both are used in arthritis rehabilitation — passive keeps joints supple; active builds strength.

## Physiotherapy triage | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/physiotherapy-triage
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is physiotherapy triage?
A: Physiotherapy triage: Physiotherapy triage is an initial assessment (often by a First Contact Practitioner in general practice) to sort MSK problems into: self-management, physio treatment, imaging, or specialist referral. Reduces GP burden and speeds care.

## PIP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/pip
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is pip?
A: PIP: PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Assessed on functional impact, not diagnosis. Arthritis frequently qualifies; Citizens Advice offers free application help.

## Pregabalin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/pregabalin
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is pregabalin?
A: Pregabalin: Pregabalin (Lyrica) is used for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia. Controlled drug in UK — slow to increase, slow to reduce. Side effects: drowsiness, weight gain, dependence risk.

## Prolotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/prolotherapy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is prolotherapy?
A: Prolotherapy: Prolotherapy injects irritant solutions (often dextrose) around tendons or joints to stimulate healing. Evidence is preliminary and mixed. Not routinely available on NHS. Sometimes offered privately for chronic joint pain.

## Proprioception: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/proprioception
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is proprioception?
A: Proprioception: Proprioception is your brain's awareness of joint position without looking. Arthritis and joint injury impair proprioception, worsening balance and falls risk. Specific balance and coordination exercises restore it.

## PRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/prp
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is prp?
A: PRP: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections use concentrated platelets from your own blood to promote tissue healing. Evidence for arthritis is emerging but not strong enough for routine NHS use. Common in private sports medicine.

## Radiofrequency denervation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is radiofrequency denervation?
A: Radiofrequency denervation: Radiofrequency denervation heats specific nerves to disrupt pain signals from spinal facet joints. Considered by NICE for carefully selected patients with confirmed facet-joint pain who haven't responded to other treatments.

## Range of motion (ROM) | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/range-of-motion
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is range of motion (rom)?
A: Range of motion (ROM): ROM is the measurable extent of movement at a joint — flexion, extension, rotation. Physiotherapists compare your ROM to normal ranges and track improvement. Regular gentle movement preserves ROM even in painful joints.

## Raynaud's phenomenon | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/raynauds
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is raynaud's phenomenon?
A: Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's is exaggerated cold response — fingers/toes turn white, then blue, then red. Primary Raynaud's is common and benign. Secondary Raynaud's is linked to autoimmune conditions (scleroderma, lupus) and needs specialist review.

## Remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/remission
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is remission?
A: Remission: Remission means very low or absent disease activity, measured by symptoms and blood markers. In RA, drug-induced remission is now a realistic goal with early DMARDs. Medication is usually continued even during remission to prevent flares.

## Rheumatoid factor | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/rheumatoid-factor
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is rheumatoid factor?
A: Rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an antibody detected in roughly 70-80% of people with rheumatoid arthritis. Can also be positive in other conditions (Sjögren's, chronic infections) and in ~5% of healthy older adults, so it's diagnostic only with symptoms.

## RICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/rice-protocol
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is rice?
A: RICE: RICE is the classic first-aid protocol for acute joint injury: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Recent evidence (PEACE and LOVE) suggests early gentle movement may be preferable to prolonged rest, but RICE remains a useful starting point.

## Rituximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/rituximab
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is rituximab?
A: Rituximab: Rituximab depletes B lymphocytes, given as hospital infusions typically every 6 months. Used when TNF-blockers fail or aren't suitable. Requires screening for hepatitis B and monitoring for infection risk.

## Sarcopenia: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/sarcopenia
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is sarcopenia?
A: Sarcopenia: Sarcopenia is accelerated muscle loss with age, worsened by inactivity and low protein intake. Reversible with resistance training and adequate protein (~1.0-1.2 g/kg/day). Contributes to falls and frailty.

## Self-referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/self-referral
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is self-referral?
A: Self-referral: Self-referral means going directly to an NHS service without a GP letter. Common for MSK physiotherapy, IAPT/Talking Therapies and sexual health. Search 'NHS [service] self referral [your area]'. Saves both your and your GP's time.

## Septic arthritis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/septic-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is septic arthritis?
A: Septic arthritis: Septic arthritis is bacterial infection of a joint, causing severe pain, swelling, redness, warmth and fever. Requires emergency hospital treatment: joint drainage and IV antibiotics. Delay can destroy the joint within days.

## Seronegative: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/seronegative
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is seronegative?
A: Seronegative: Seronegative arthritis means inflammatory joint disease without positive RF or anti-CCP tests. Includes AS, PsA, reactive arthritis. Diagnosis relies on clinical picture and imaging; management is similar to seropositive disease.

## Shared decision-making | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/shared-decision-making
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is shared decision-making?
A: Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a formal NHS approach where clinicians present options and patients contribute values and preferences to reach a treatment plan. Especially important in arthritis where multiple options fit different lifestyles.

## Sjögren's syndrome | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/sjogrens
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is sjögren's syndrome?
A: Sjögren's syndrome: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks moisture-producing glands, causing dry eyes and mouth. Often coexists with RA and lupus. Managed with tear substitutes, saliva stimulants and immunosuppression when needed.

## Spinal fusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/spinal-fusion
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is spinal fusion?
A: Spinal fusion: Spinal fusion joins two or more vertebrae together to stop movement causing pain. Considered for specific structural problems (severe instability, deformity). Not a routine treatment for chronic non-specific back pain.

## Stem cell therapy | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/stem-cell
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is stem cell therapy?
A: Stem cell therapy: Stem cell therapy for arthritis remains experimental. Regulatory framework is tight. Beware of overseas clinics making strong claims. UK approved treatments are limited to specific research settings.

## Subchondral bone: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/subchondral
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is subchondral bone?
A: Subchondral bone: Subchondral bone lies immediately beneath the joint cartilage. In OA, it thickens ('sclerosis'), may develop small holes ('cysts') and gets damaged as cartilage thins. Changes are visible on X-ray and are diagnostic.

## Sulfasalazine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/sulfasalazine
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is sulfasalazine?
A: Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine is a well-established DMARD used for RA and some spondyloarthropathies. Taken as tablets. Common in the UK because it's affordable and safe in pregnancy (unlike methotrexate). Can cause harmless orange discolouration of urine and skin.

## Synovium: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/synovium
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is synovium?
A: Synovium: The synovium is the thin membrane lining the inside of a joint capsule. It produces synovial fluid, which lubricates and nourishes cartilage. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the synovium, causing swelling, warmth and long-term joint damage.

## TENS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/tens
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is tens?
A: TENS: TENS units deliver small electrical pulses through skin electrodes to block pain signals. Available from pharmacies for £20-50. Evidence in chronic arthritis pain is modest but many people find them helpful, with no side effects.

## Tocilizumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/tocilizumab
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is tocilizumab?
A: Tocilizumab: Tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6, used in RA, giant cell arteritis and juvenile arthritis. Available as subcutaneous injection or IV infusion. Requires regular blood monitoring.

## Tophi: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/tophi
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is tophi?
A: Tophi: Tophi are visible or palpable lumps of urate crystals in the skin, ears, tendons or joints in long-standing gout. They cause deformity and joint damage. Their presence means urate-lowering therapy is essential.

## Tramadol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/tramadol
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is tramadol?
A: Tramadol: Tramadol is a controlled painkiller for moderate pain. Interacts with many antidepressants and can lower seizure threshold. Long-term use in chronic pain is discouraged by current NHS guidance.

## Triple therapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/triple-therapy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is triple therapy?
A: Triple therapy: Triple therapy typically means methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, an evidence-based combination for people with RA whose disease isn't controlled on methotrexate alone. Cheaper alternative to biologics with comparable outcomes for some patients.

## Ultrasound: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/ultrasound
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is ultrasound?
A: Ultrasound: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints, tendons and inflammation in real time. Increasingly used by rheumatologists for early RA detection and injection guidance.

## Uric acid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/uric-acid
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is uric acid?
A: Uric acid: Uric acid is a natural waste product of purine breakdown. High blood levels ('hyperuricaemia') can crystallise in joints, causing gout attacks. Managed by lowering intake (alcohol, offal, seafood) and, when attacks recur, urate-lowering drugs (allopurinol).

## Uveitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/uveitis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is uveitis?
A: Uveitis: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye's uveal tract, causing pain, redness and blurred vision. Strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies. Any red painful eye with AS needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.

## Weight loss for arthritis | Arthritis Glossary
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What is weight loss for arthritis?
A: Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain. Every 1 kg lost cuts knee load by about 4 kg during walking. Combine with strength work to protect muscle mass.

## Arthritis Guides Hub | Living With Arthritis UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: Where can I find UK arthritis guides?
A: The Living With Arthritis UK guides hub collects practical pages on PIP and benefits, exercise, diet, pain relief and NHS care. Each guide is written for people in the United Kingdom and reviewed against current clinical guidance.

## Arthritis Pain Relief: What Works | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/arthritis-pain-relief
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: How do I relieve arthritis pain?
A: First-line pain relief includes paracetamol, topical NSAID gels and heat/cold packs. Exercise reduces pain more than most drugs long-term. If pain persists, your GP can consider oral NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections or, for inflammatory arthritis, DMARDs.

## Arthritis vs Fibromyalgia | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: How do I know if it's arthritis or fibromyalgia?
A: Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-processing condition — pain and tenderness spread across the body, plus fatigue, poor sleep and 'fibro fog', with normal joint examination and imaging. It's common to have both. Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is clinical, based on ACR criteria.
Q: When would you pick Arthritis?
A: Localised joint pain; visible swelling; imaging changes; morning stiffness in specific joints.
Q: When would you pick Fibromyalgia?
A: Widespread body pain; tenderness on touch; fatigue; sleep issues; 'fibro fog'.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Both respond to graded exercise, sleep hygiene and CBT — different medications from your GP.

## UK Arthritis Benefits & PIP Guide | Living With Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/benefits-pip
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: Can you claim PIP for arthritis?
A: Yes. Personal Independence Payment is not awarded for a diagnosis but for how arthritis affects daily living and mobility. Under State Pension age you claim PIP (Adult Disability Payment in Scotland); over it, Attendance Allowance. If you are refused, ask for a mandatory reconsideration within one month, then appeal to a tribunal.

## Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Do I qualify for a Blue Badge with arthritis?
A: A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affects walking. You automatically qualify if you get the higher-rate mobility component of PIP or DLA; otherwise you can apply on 'discretionary' grounds by describing how far and comfortably you can walk. Local council disability parking bays and hospital blue-zone bays are separate schemes.
Q: When would you pick Blue Badge?
A: Severe walking difficulty; qualifies for higher-rate PIP mobility; nationwide use.
Q: When would you pick Local disabled parking?
A: Occasional need close to home/work; council-specific bays; supplements a Blue Badge.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Renewal is every 3 years and the fee is £10 in England, free in Wales and Scotland.

## Improving Bone Density & Osteoporosis | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: How do I improve bone density?
A: Weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing), resistance training, calcium 700 mg/day and vitamin D 10 mcg/day support bone density. If your FRAX score is high, your GP may prescribe bisphosphonates.

## Bursitis vs Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is it bursitis or arthritis?
A: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a fluid sac that cushions between joints and tendons, most often in the shoulder, hip or knee. Pain is usually localised, worse with pressure and movement in a specific direction. Arthritis pain is inside the joint. Bursitis often responds well to rest, ice, NSAIDs and a targeted injection; arthritis is a longer-term condition needing a treatment plan.
Q: When would you pick Bursitis?
A: Sudden onset; tender to touch over a specific spot; pain when lying on that side.
Q: When would you pick Arthritis?
A: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; imaging changes; pattern typical of OA or RA.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Repeated bursitis in the same joint can suggest underlying arthritis — worth investigating.

## Can Exercise Make Osteoarthritis Worse? | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis-worse
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse?
A: No — done correctly, exercise reduces OA pain and slows progression. Some soreness during and up to 2 hours after exercise is normal. Sharp, sudden or persistent pain lasting more than 24 hours means you've done too much; scale back but don't stop.

## Chair Yoga vs Tai Chi for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I try chair yoga or tai chi for arthritis?
A: Both are excellent low-impact options with strong evidence in older adults. Chair yoga is more accessible if standing is painful or unsafe — you can do it from a stable chair with no equipment. Tai chi requires standing balance but has the strongest evidence for reducing falls in older adults with arthritis (roughly 30% fewer falls in NHS-endorsed trials).
Q: When would you pick Chair yoga?
A: Severe knee/hip pain; poor balance; can't stand for long; recovering from surgery.
Q: When would you pick Tai chi?
A: You can stand safely; want falls-prevention benefit; enjoy a group class.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Look for instructors trained in adaptations for arthritis — search 'arthritis-adapted' or 'senior-focused'.

## Cold Plunge vs Warm Bath for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is a cold plunge or warm bath better for arthritis?
A: For arthritis, a warm bath is safer and better-evidenced than cold plunging. Warm water eases stiffness, relaxes muscle tension around joints, and supports gentle movement. Cold plunging is trending but the evidence in arthritis is very limited, and it can trigger flare-ups in inflammatory conditions, worsen Raynaud's, and be dangerous for people with heart conditions.
Q: When would you pick Warm bath / hydrotherapy pool (33-36°C)?
A: Stiffness; RA/OA; muscle tension; before or after exercise.
Q: When would you pick Cold plunge (<15°C)?
A: Not recommended for most arthritis. If you want cold exposure, use targeted ice packs on inflamed joints only.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Never cold plunge if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, Raynaud's, or you're pregnant, without medical advice.

## UK Disability Support for Arthritis | Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/disability-support
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What UK disability support is available for arthritis?
A: You may qualify for Personal Independence Payment (PIP), Blue Badge, Access to Work grants, and workplace reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010. Citizens Advice and Versus Arthritis helpline (0800 5200 520) guide applications.

## DMARDs vs Biologics for Rheumatoid Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/dmards-vs-biologics
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What's the difference between DMARDs and biologics?
A: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide) are the first-line drugs for RA and other inflammatory arthritis — cheap, taken by mouth, and effective for the majority of people. Biologics (adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab and others) are injected or infused, target specific parts of the immune system, and are added when DMARDs alone aren't enough. NHS NICE guidance sets clear criteria for stepping up.
Q: When would you pick Conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate)?
A: First-line for RA, PsA, some other inflammatory arthritis; NICE requires trying these first.
